relations.subject: sgw:channel-cmd
relations.evidence: By default, every document in the collection is automatically assigned to a channel with the same name as the collection.

relations.subject: sgw:channel
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: minted - channels have no separate create-time API call the way roles/users do (see access-control-how-create-roles.json's createdVia); a channel simply comes into existence the first time a document is routed to it
relations.evidence: Channels are created as documents are assigned to them.

relations.subject: sgw:channel
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: minted - a syntactic constraint on the grant/routing key itself, a concern that doesn't arise for server/'s or Capella's closed-enum privilege/role names
relations.evidence: Valid channel names consist of text letters [A–Z, a–z], digits [0–9], and a few special characters [= + / . , _ @]. Channel names are case-sensitive. Channels with no documents assigned to them are empty.

relations.subject: sgw:channel
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: minted - ties the channel concept to its documented scale guidance
relations.evidence:
Channels per document | ... | 50
Channels per user | ... | 1,000

relations.subject: sgw:channel-limits
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused (minted above) - the per-document/per-user channel-count guidance is itself derived from the harder metadata-size ceiling
relations.evidence: The amount of memory consumed by the combined number of channels and access grants must fit within the maximum 1Mb xattr size limit.

relations.subject: sgw:channel
relations.evidence: Every time a document is assigned to a new channel, the channel name is appended to that document's sync metadata. Therefore, a document's set of channels is limited by the allowed sync metadata size.

relations.subject: sgw:channel-cmd
relations.evidence: You assign a document to the public (!) channel using the channel() function. Documents assigned to this channel can be accessed by all users; even users assigned no specific channel access.

relations.subject: sgw:all-documents-channel
relations.evidence: This channel should not be confused with the use of the All Channels Wildcard in access grants.

relations.subject: sgw:access-cmd
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused (grantsChannelAccess) - here the object is the wildcard grant target rather than a specific channel
relations.evidence: You make dynamic user access grants in the sync function using the access() method. Granting a user access with the all channels wildcard gives them access to any channel.

relations.subject: sgw:all-channels-wildcard
relations.evidence: Users granted access using the all channels wildcard do not inherit requireAccess() rights to any specific channel.

relations.subject: sgw:admin-channels-property
relations.evidence: Using the Admin REST API: You can provide the admin_channels property within the collection_access property using the Admin REST API endpoint.

cross_product_finding: This page's Channel Limits / Sync Metadata Limits sections surface a category of access-control-adjacent concern that simply does not exist for server/'s privilege model or Capella's role model in the prior batches: RESOURCE COST OF THE GRANT ITSELF. Because every channel a document belongs to is materialized as metadata replicated alongside that document (appended to sync metadata, capped at 1 MB or 20 MB depending on enable_shared_bucket_access, with guidance limits of 50 channels/document and 1,000 channels/user), the access-control model has a direct, quantified storage/bandwidth cost that scales with how finely you partition data into channels. A server/ privilege check or a Capella role check costs nothing extra per row/document - it's a lookup against a fixed table at query/API-call time. SGW's channel check is comparatively 'free' at read time (simple set intersection) but the GRANT DATA ITSELF is expensive to create and store, and that cost is a first-class documented constraint. This reinforces the batch's central finding: SGW's access control is not a permission-check system layered on top of otherwise-unaffected data, it is baked into the document's own replicated metadata, with real storage and revocation (auto-purge) consequences that neither prior batch's model has to contend with.
